items.e: The word of Abram, the prisoner of hope; Who loosened his bowstring ( yitro ).
Half of his courage is forever gone; And the rest ( yitro ) was dissipated by his tortuous wanderings.
This is a comment upon the chapter Which opens with the word Yitro (Jethro).

NOW JETHRO HEARD. Scripture notes above the incident of Amalek because Amalek came to Rephidim. Now the chapter that opens with the words In the third month (Ex. 19:1) should have followed the incident of Amalek, for Scripture states there, And when they were departed from Rephidim, and were come to the wilderness of Sinai (Ex. 19:2). This being the case, why was the account of Jethro inserted between these two chapters? Saadiah Gaon says that Jethro came to the wilderness of Sinai before the giving of the Torah. However, I believe that Jethro came to Sinai in the second year, after the erection of the tabernacle. For the chapter speaks of a burnt-offering and sacrifices for God (v. 12), and it does not mention that he built a new altar. Furthermore, Scripture writes, and I make them know the statutes of God, and His laws (v. 16). Now this took place after the giving of the Torah. True proof that my words are correct is the fact that Scripture clearly states, where he was encamped, at the mount of God (v. 5). Now Moses spoke to Hobab, the latter being Jethro as I explained in the Torah portion These Are The Names . For Moses’ father-in-law does not refer to Reuel, which precedes the term father-in-law, but refers to Hobab. Scripture clearly states, from the children of Hobab the father-in-law of Moses (Jud. 4:11). Moses told Hobab, [ Leave us not, I pray thee ] forasmuch as thou knowest how we are to encamp in the wilderness (Num. 10:31). Now we know that Israel camped around Sinai for about a year. Lo and behold, Moses’ very words prove this to be so. For Moses is quoted in the Torah portion, These are the words as saying, The Lord our God spoke unto us in Horeb, saying: …turn you, and take your journey (Deut. 1:6,7). Now this was said close to their time of journey. Moses continued, And I spoke unto you at that time saying: I am not able to bear you myself alone (Deut. 1:9); for the Lord your God hath multiplied you, and, behold, ye are this day as the stars of heaven for multitude (Deut. 1:10). The reason Moses mentioned this to them was that God told Jacob, Behold, I will make thee fruitful, and multiply thee, and I will make of thee a company of peoples; and will give this land to thy seed after thee for an everlasting possession (Gen. 48:4). Now the meaning of the latter is: when your seed increase I will give them the land. Moses therefore said, the Lord your God hath multiplied you and the time for you to inherit the land has come. However, since you are so numerous I was not able to carry you alone, and I had to place over you captains of thousands and captains of hundreds. Now this was the advice given to Moses by Jethro on the morrow following his coming to the wilderness of Sinai. Moses therefore said to Hobab, who, as we explained, is to be identified with Jethro, We are journeying (Num. 10:29). Hobab responded, I will not go; but I will depart to mine own land, and to my kindred (Num. 10:30). This is what And Moses let his father-in-law depart; and he went his way into his own land (v. 27) refers to. I will now explain why the chapter dealing with Jethro was inserted here. It was placed here because Scripture had just mentioned the evil that Amalek did to Israel. The Torah wants to contrast it with the good that Jethro rendered Israel. Scripture notes, And Jethro rejoiced for all the goodness which the Lord had done to Israel (v. 9) and that he gave proper and correct counsel to Moses and Israel. Moses told Jethro, and thou shalt be to us instead of eyes (Num. 10:31), meaning that he enlightened their eyes. King Saul similarly said, for ye showed kindness to all the children of Israel (I Sam. 15:6). Now because Scripture states in the preceding chapter, the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Ex. 17:16), namely, that when God gives Israel rest they are obligated to wage war against Amalek, the Torah mentions the account of Jethro. For the descendants of Jethro lived in proximity to the nation of Amalek, and the Torah wants Israel to remember the kindness that Jethro demonstrated so that they do not harm his seed. Thus we find the Rechabites, who were descended from Jethro, living among the children of Israel in Jerusalem. We find Jonadab the son of Rechab in the time of Jeremiah (Jer. 35:19). There is another chapter similar to the one above.
ALL THAT GOD ( ELOHIM ) HAD DONE. Scripture employs the name of God that was known in the world before the appearance of Moses, for all admitted that God existed.

AND FOR ISRAEL HIS PEOPLE. God’s people, or the people of Moses. It is possible that the lamed should be translated as “because,” that is, because of Moses and Israel, the reference being to the plagues and the drowning of Pharaoh.
HOW THAT THE LORD ( YHVH ) HAD BROUGHT. Scripture employs the divine name revealed to Moses, since it was through the miracles that Israel went out of Egypt.
AND JETHRO TOOK. Scripture reads, Moses’ wife, and not Jethro’s daughter, because Moses was more important than her father’s house.

AFTER HE HAD SENT HER AWAY. Some say that Moses gave her permission to return to her father’s house, at the lodging place, prior to his returning alone to Egypt. Other say she sent gifts to Moses. Compare, shilluchim (gifts) in gifts unto his daughter (I Kings 9:16).

AND. Note that those who speak the holy tongue preserve the verbal forms in all conjugations. However, they are not careful to do so with proper nouns. Therefore do not be amazed that Moses called his son Gershom because he lived ( gar ) there ( sham ). For look, kayin (Cain) was so called because Eve said, kaniti (I have gotten) (Gen. 4:1). However, this is grammatically incorrect. The name Noah, which Scripture derives from yenachamenu (shall comfort us) (Gen. 5:28), is even more difficult. Scripture at times inverts a name. Thus Hushim (Gen. 46:23) and Shuham (Num. 26:42) are one and the same. Yabetz (Jabez) was so called because his mother bore him in pain ( otzev ). Sometimes a letter is dropped in a name, as in the case of Maacah which is a variant of Micah. The reverse is true of Yov (Iob) (Gen. 46:13), which is the same as Yashuv (Jashub) (Num. 26:24). Many say it is the same with Shemu’el (Samuel), which is derived from she’iltihu (I have asked him) (I Sam. 1:20). However, in my opinion a shuruk has been substituted here for a cholam, as in the case of Tohu (I Sam. 1:1) and Toah (I Chron. 6:19); Zuph (I Sam. 1:1) and Zophai (I Chron. 6:11); Nun (Ex. 33:11) and Non (I Chron. 7:26). Now Shemu’el (Samuel) comes from shemo el (his name is God). Samuel’s mother called him by God’s name because the Lord answered her request. Do not be amazed that a human being should be called by God’s name, for, observe, we find this to be the case with the name Zurishaddai (Num. 7:36). There are many other similar instances. In my opinion the altar which Moses built was similarly called Adonai-nissi (the Lord is my banner) (Ex. 17:15). Likewise, the name of the Messiah will be called Adonai-tzidkenu (the Lord is our righteousness) (Jer. 23:6). However, Rabbi Saadiah Gaon says that God’s name is connected to the word yikre’o (shall call him) and the name of the Messiah will be tzidkenu (our righteousness). Now its correct interpretation is in keeping with the opinion of the master of the cantillical notes, who placed a tircha in the word yikre’o . For there is a great difference between va-yikra be-shem Adonai (and called upon the name of the Lord) (Gen. 12:8), written in connection with Abraham with a tircha beneath the word va-yikra , and vayikra ve-shem Adonai (and proclaimed the name of the Lord) (Ex. 34:5) which is written in the Book of Moses as I will explain in its place.

AND THE NAME OF THE OTHER WAS. It is the custom in Hebrew to say, “This is how the second one was called.” At other times it uses the term “the one,” as in and the name of one was Bozez, and the name of the other was Seneh (I Sam. 14:4).

[FOR THE GOD OF MY FATHER WAS MY HELP.] The word amar (he said), which should have followed the word ki (for), has been omitted in for the God of my father. Scripture does not read, “for he said the God of my father was my help” because the phrase refers to for he said: I have been a stranger (v. 3), which is written above. It is similar to for God hath made me fruitful (Gen. 41:52). I have already explained why Moses named his younger son Eliezer.
AND CAME. Scripture notes that Jethro followed etiquette when he came to Moses. Jethro went first, the sons of Moses went behind him, and after them Moses’ wife, as is the custom.
WHERE HE WAS ENCAMPED. He encamped there for many days.

AND HE SAID UNTO MOSES. He had already said unto Moses prior to his coming, via an agent or by a written message: I thy father-in-law Jethro am coming unto thee, and also thy wife, who is uppermost in importance, and her two sons who are coming with her.

AND MOSES WENT OUT TO MEET HIS FATHER-IN-LAW. Out of regard for Jethro and his wisdom, but not out of regard for his wife and children, for it is not customary for a respected person to go out to meet his wife or children.

AND BOWED DOWN. Va-yishtachu (and bowed down) is grammatically difficult. We know that it comes from a root ending in a heh . The vav in va-yishtachu is in place of a heh , like the vav of shalev (at ease) in I was at ease (Job 16:12), from whose root we get the word shalavti (at ease) in I was not at ease (Job 3:26). Now the term va-yishtachaveh should have been employed in the singular, rather than va-yishtachu, for the tav is a sign of the hitpa’el conjugation. It is like the tav in mishta’eh (steadfastly) in And the man looked steadfastly on her (Gen. 24:21). For the rule relating to the dentals states that if the first letter of a root before which the tav of the hitpa’el conjugation is placed is a dental, then [the tav is placed after the first root letter]. Now because the heh has been changed into a vav in va-yishtachu Hebrew allows the first vav, which is not a plural suffix, to remain in place of the root heh and silences the vav . Hence the word reads va-yishtachu. Now a vav at the end of a word is the sign of the plural suffix when silent as in titra’u (look one upon the other) in Why do ye look one upon the other (Gen. 42:1). Thus the word va-yishtachu, ending in a silent vav, would appear to be in the plural. Va-yishtachu was therefore penultimately accented to differentiate between it and the customary way of vocalizing plurals.
[AND BOWED DOWN.] Logically speaking, the one who goes out is the one who bows to his counterpart.
[EACH OTHER.] Scripture refers to Jethro as Moses’ friend because of his greatness in wisdom.
AND THEY CAME INTO THE TENT. Which was known as Moses’ tent.
AND MOSES TOLD. This verse indicates that the meaning of for Moses, and for Israel (v. 1) is: because of them.

THE TRAVAIL. Tela’ah (travail) comes from the same root as ve-nilu (shall loathe) in and the Egyptians shall loathe (Ex. 7:18). The tav is superfluous. Its meaning is, an affliction which a person is unable to bear or verbalize. It refers to Egypt’s pursuit of Israel at the sea, the war with Amalek, and the thirst and hunger which the congregation suffered. God delivered them from all of these.

AND JETHRO REJOICED. Va-yichad (rejoiced) comes from the same root as the word chedvah (rejoicing). It should have been vocalized like the word va-yift (enticed) in And my heart hath been secretly enticed (Job 31:27) and va-yishb (and took captive) in and took some of them captive (Num. 21:1). However, the chet was vocalized with a pattach because it is a guttural, and the dagesh remains in the dalet as it was. I am not aware of a letter having a dagesh at the end of a word in all of Scripture except in the case of a bet, gimel, dalet, kaf, peh, tav at the end of a word when two sheva’im come together, as in the word va-yishb (and took captive) in and took some of them captive (Num. 21:1) and va-yesht (and he drank) in And he drank of the wine (Gen. 9:21). However, we never find a dagesh at the end of a word when preceded by a vowel except in the case of a pattach. In the latter case we find two such words namely, va-yichad (rejoiced) in And Jethro rejoiced and yichad (rejoice) in Let it not rejoice among the days of the year (Job 3:6).

AND JETHRO SAID: BLESSED BE THE LORD. Give your attention to the grammatical explanation of the word barukh (blessed). Note that the pa’ul can only be formed from transitive verbs. If you find a verb following the pa’ul form, look around; if you find it has a transitive po’el form, then the word is a real pa’ul. However, if you do not find it to be so, then the word is an adjective. Similarly, if a word is in the po’el form and its root does not come in the pa’ul in the same conjugation, then the word is also not a po’el but an adjective. For example, the po’el and pa’ul forms of shamar (kept) are shomer (keeps) and shamur (kept). Compare, shamur in riches kept by the owner thereof to his hurt (Eccles. 5:12). Now we encounter holekh (goes), omed (stands), yotze (goes out). All these words appear to be verbs in the po’el, for they follow the form of shomer. However, since these roots form intransitive verbs, for one cannot say halukh (wented), amud (stooded up), yatzu (wented out), these words do not come in the pa’ul. Therefore when Scripture uses the term holekh (went) in because he went (Num. 22:21), it employs an adjective, not a verb. We find [Scripture using] the word atzum (mighty). The word appears to be a pa’ul because it follows the paradigm of shamur (kept). However, when we investigated this root we found the word va-ya’atzmu (waxed mighty), in and multiplied, and waxed exceedingly mighty (Ex. 1:7), to be among the intransitive verbs. For its transitive form comes in the hifil as in va-ya’atzimehu (and made them too mighty) in and made them too mighty for their adversaries (Ps. 105:24). Now we cannot say that otzem (strengthens) following the paradigm of shomer (keeps) means strength, for in this case it has a different meaning, as in otzem (shutteth) in And shutteth his eyes from looking upon evil (Is. 33:15). Now we find the word barukh, which follows the paradigm of shamur (kept). We searched all of Scripture and we did not see this root used with this meaning in all of the kal conjugation. We found it used only with another meaning, namely, to kneel, as in va-yivrakh (kneeled) in and kneeled down upon his knees (I Chron. 6:13), which is also intransitive and does not have a pa’ul form. The word barukh (blessed) is thus like the word atzum (might), a kal adjective. Rabbi Merinus says that barukh (blessed) is an adjective in the pi’el. Its resh should have received a dagesh like all other such roots, such as berekh (curse) in Naboth did curse (I Kings 21:13). Barukh follows the paradigm of shakkul (bereaved) in as a bear that is bereaved of her whelps (Hos. 13:8). However, Rabbi Merinus spoke incorrectly, for all adjectives such as shakkul (bereaved), gibbor (warrior), shikkor (drunk) do not undergo any change by having the vowel that precedes the dagesh change in the singular construct or in the plural. Compare, gibbor (mighty man) in And Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim (II Chron. 28:7), and gibborim (mighty) in Woe unto them that are mighty (Is. 5:22). Now the word berukh (blessed of), in Come in, thou blessed of the Lord (Gen. 24:31) and berukhim (blessed) in, Blessed be ye of the Lord (Ps. 115:15), argue against Rabbi Merinus.

WHO HATH DELIVERED YOU. He said this to Moses and Aaron, who were God’s messengers and through whom the plagues came upon Pharaoh and Egypt. Jethro therefore said, out of the hand of the Egyptians, and out of the hand of Pharaoh. After this he blessed the Lord, who hath delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians in Egypt and at the splitting of the Red Sea.
NOW I KNOW. I have explained the meaning of now I know in the Torah portion Shemot, in the verse and they shall say to me: What is His name? (Ex. 3:13).

[YEA, FOR THAT.] Because of the fact that the Egyptians dealt willfully with Israel. Jethro similarly, noted above, I know that the Lord is greater than all gods in that he punished the Egyptians because they made Israel work with rigor. It is similarly written, Thou knewest that they dealt proudly (hezidu) against them (Neh. 9:11) that is, they behaved like a person who does whatever he wants to. Scripture already stated, for I know their pains; and I am come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians (Ex. 3:7,8).
AND JETHRO, MOSES’ FATHER-IN-LAW, TOOK A BURNT-OFFERING AND SACRIFICES. The latter refers to peace-offerings.
[FOR GOD.] The meaning of for God is that henceforth the revered Lord shall be his God.
AND AARON CAME, AND ALL THE ELDERS OF ISRAEL. There is no need to mention Moses, as they were in Moses’ tent.
TO EAT BREAD. Peaceofferings.
[BEFORE GOD.] Scripture reads thus because Moses’ tent was on the east side of the tabernacle.
AND IT CAME TO PASS ON THE MORROW. Of Jethro’s coming.
THAT MOSES SAT. As was his custom.

FROM THE MORNING UNTO THE EVENING. Note that true morning begins with sunrise. The term morning is, as I have previously noted, also applied to the breaking of dawn, when light begins to be seen in the clouds. In the latter instance the term is artificially used. Similarly, true evening begins when the sun sets. The term is also artificially applied up to the time that the light sets. David similarly said, The sun ariseth, they slink away (Ps. 104:22). Scripture then states, Man goeth forth unto his work, And to his labor until the evening (Ps. 104:23). It is therefore fitting to interpret from even unto even, shall ye keep your sabbath (Lev. 23:32) to mean: from the true evening to the true evening. However, our sages of blessed memory “added from the weekday to the holy day” and said that the Sabbath does not end until the stars come out. It is thus fitting from the Torah’s point of view to start the Sabbath at sunset. All scientists and astronomers admit that the day’s boundary is the moment when the circle of the sun faces all over the area of the earth. This starts at sunrise and ends at sunset.
AND…SAW ALL THAT HE DID TO THE PEOPLE. That he caused them to stand from morning to evening.

Rabbi Solomon says that Jethro reacted in this manner because Moses alone sat and Israel stood, the latter being improper. There can be no doubt that Moses’ station was too great for Jethro to say this. For behold, Aaron, who was a great man in the eyes of Israel and was older than Moses, said to Moses, Oh my lord (Num. 12:11). Moses acted in the proper manner, for the judge sits and the litigants stand. We thus read, then both the men, between whom the controversy is, shall stand (Deut. 19:17). Jethro said, why to Moses for no reason other than that Moses was sitting alone and had no other judges to assist him. [WHY.] Rabbi Merinus says that the word maddu’a (why) is similar to mallakhem (what mean ye) (Is. 3:15) and to mazzeh (what is that) in what is that in thy hand (Ex. 4:2), each of which is a compound of two words. The same is true of maddu’a, which means: what is in your mind that you do this?

AND MOSES SAID. Moses answered, I do two things. One, Because the people come unto me to inquire of God, that is, to inquire of God’s law. The other, when they have a matter, it cometh unto me (v. 16). Moses explained the second task first, namely, and I judge between a man and his neighbor ( ibid .); and, he then said, to one who inquires, I make them know the statutes of God.

AND…SAID…THE THING THAT THOU DOEST IS NOT GOOD. In my eyes. Jethro then explained himself, Thou wilt surely wear away. Navol tibbol (thou shalt surely wear away) comes from the same root as yibbol (wither) in And whose leaf doth not wither (Ps. 1:3) and novelet (fadeth) in For ye shall be as a terebinth whose leaf fadeth (Is. 1:30). Its meaning is, you shall, as it were, drop like a withered leaf. The word gam (both) is to be prefaced also to for the thing is too heavy for thee .
TO PERFORM IT. Asohu (to perform it) is grammatically inconsistent. It follows the form of lishmerehu (to preserve him), for we do not find the heh to be visible in the root ayin, sin, heh .
HEARKEN NOW UNTO MY VOICE, I WILL GIVE THEE COUNCIL. I’atzekha, means I will give you council.

[GOD.] Note that the term Elohim (God) is, as I have noted, an adjective. It is only because the word is used often that this adjective is considered as if it were a proper noun. Examples of the latter are: Elohim (God) in God will let me gaze upon my adversaries (Ps. 59:11); In the beginning God (Elohim) created the heaven and the earth (Gen. 1:1), and many other instances. It is for this reason that our sages of blessed memory placed Elohim among the names that are not erasable.

[AND GOD BE WITH THEE.] Its meaning is, God will help you if you act in this manner. At the close of his words, Jethro told Moses to ask permission of God to act in accordance with Jethro’s counsel. This is what Jethro meant by and God command thee so (v. 23). There is no doubt that Moses did so.
[BE THOU FOR THE PEOPLE.] The meaning of la-am is, for the people.
BEFORE GOD. From God’s side.

AND BRING THOU THE CAUSES UNTO GOD. If they be difficult. These are the things that Moses mentioned at first, viz., when they have a matter, it cometh unto me (v. 16). Jethro then explained this to him, viz., the hard causes they shall bring unto thee.

AND THOU SHALT TEACH THEM. As to the second thing you spoke of, you are obligated to teach and instruct them only those things that they are uncertain of. For it takes great effort to teach all, the work that they must do. Now as to the meaning of ve-hizharta (and thou shalt teach): ve-hizharta comes from the same root as nizhar in and took not warning (Ezek. 33:5). Nizhar means took warning.
THEM. Ethem (them) is a compound of two words.

[AND THOU SHALT TEACH THEM.] You shall warn them to observe the positive and negative commandments that are tied to the heart, such as, to love God, to cleave unto God, to fear God, to walk after God, to circumcise the foreskin of the heart, not to hate one’s brother, not to take revenge, and not to bear a grudge. They are the most important commandments. Moses similarly said, [ But the word is very nigh unto thee ] in thy mouth, and in thy heart, that thou mayest do it (Deut. 30:14). There many such precepts.
THEY MUST WALK. Yelekhu bah means wherein they must walk.

AND THE WORK THAT THEY MUST DO. The reference is to positive precepts which are observed by action. Most of them are not positive commandments that stand by themselves but serve as a reminder, such as the Sabbath, the Festivals, the redemption of the first-born, loving the stranger, the fringes, the tefillin , the mezuzah , and also the prohibition against mixing linen and wool, and many others. I will explain them in their place.

MOREOVER THOU SHALT PROVIDE. I have already informed you that the speakers of Hebrew do not preserve exact wording. They only preserve meanings. Hence, as I will yet explain, we will not pay attention to whether the text is full or deficient. Now when Moses recounted this incident, in place of able men he said, Get you…men (Deut. 1:13). Men in the latter verse has the same meaning as men in Choose us out men (Ex. 17:9) and in all of them men (Num. 13:3). Jethro said appoint men.

SUCH AS FEAR GOD. Who do not fear men but fear only God. It was to them that Moses was referring when he said, wise…and understanding (Deut. 1:13). For it is not possible for one to be a fearer of heaven unless one be wise.

Jethro continued: MEN OF TRUTH. Who do not lie. HATING UNJUST GAIN ( betza ). Money. People who appear so, and are known as such by the community. It was in reference to these that Moses said, and known (Deut. 1:13).

RULERS OF THOUSANDS. One may wonder: If the meaning of the term rulers is here to be taken literally, then their number comes to more that seventy-nine thousand. Now, it is extremely far-fetched for there to have been so many rulers. Indeed, Scripture states, For the transgression of a land many are the princes thereof (Prov. 28:2). Furthermore, how is it possible for an eighth of the camp to be heads of the tribes? For this is what Moses said, that is, So I took the heads of your tribes (Deut. 1:15). Additionally, how is it possible that all of the above-mentioned virtues were found in these people who came out of Egypt and learned their ways? Indeed, Scripture states, After the doings of the land of Egypt, wherein ye dwelt, shall ye not do (Lev. 18:3). Now the desert generation, who were taught by Moses for forty years, did not have to work, for their bread was freely given and their water faithfully delivered. The manna, which they were not in the habit of eating in Egypt, in contrast to the types of food which they desired, instilled wisdom. Nevertheless, Moses told this generation at the end of forty years, but the Lord hath not given you a heart to know, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, unto this day (Deut. 29:3). We are thus amazed as to how it was possible to find the above-noted number of wise and understanding men. It appears to me that the rulers of thousands were men who had under them a thousand people, namely, slaves, young men, or hired hands. It is possible that these were the heads of the tribes and that they numbered twelve. The rulers of hundreds were many. The rulers of fifties were so called after the manner of and fifty men to run before him (II Sam. 15:1).
AND LET THEM JUDGE THE PEOPLE. When the people have a matter. What they do not know how to judge you will judge. If you do not know it, then bring thou the causes unto God (v. 19).

THEN THOU SHALT BE ABLE. The vav of ve-yakholta (then thou shalt be able) is like the Arabic fah . If you do this thing, and God grants you permission to do it, then you will be able to endure. Now the word amod (endure) is an infinitive. It is like the word amod (stand) in Stand in the door of the tent (Jud. 4:20). Peshotah (strip you) ve-orah (and make you bare), va-chagorah (and gird) in Strip you, and make you bare, and gird sackcloth upon your lions (Is. 32:11) are also infinitives.

[AND ALL THIS PEOPLE ALSO SHALL GO TO THEIR PLACE IN PEACE.] Its meaning is, when some the disputants who were standing before Moses were not able to present their cases before him for adjudication, their conflict intensified when they returned to their tents. However, now each one would return to his place, that is, his tent, in peace.

[SO MOSES HEARKENED.] Scripture mentions Jethro’s council but does not mention Moses’ council. Moses added to Jethro’s council: that is, Moses placed officers over the tribes to enforce the decrees of the judges. Scripture thus reads, and officers, tribe by tribe (Deut. 1:15), and Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates (Deut. 16:18).

AND MOSES CHOSE ABLE MEN. This thing was ascertainable. Such as fear God is not mentioned, for only God knows what is in a person’s heart. Moses said that he chose wise men for us, for he was able to ascertain this. However, there are wise men who are not God-fearing. Moses mentioned men who are known (Deut. 1:13), that is, men whom people recognize. He did not mention them here because he was being brief.

THEY JUDGED THEMSELVES. Yishputu (judged) means the same as yishpotu (judged). A shuruk has been substituted for a cholam in yishputu. It is similar to lo ta’avuri (neither pass) in neither pass from hence (Ruth 2:5), which has the same meaning as ve-lo ta’avori (and neither pass). However, Rabbi Solomon wanted to distinguish between them but was unable to do so. Now from a grammatical standpoint the following may be said. We find the terms chadelu (ceased) and chadellu (ceased) with a dagesh in the lamed because it is marked with an etnach in The rulers ceased (chadelu) in Israel, they ceased (chadellu) (Jud. 5:7). We similarly find the word nazollu (quake) at the end of a verse in That the mountains may quake (Is. 63:19). Scripture likewise reads, tehatellu vo (will ye mock him) (Job 13:9) since tehatellu is considered to be the last word in the sentence because it is connected to the word vo, which has only one vowel. Similarly, yishpetu hem is like yishputu (hem), for one can say that the etnach does not have the same power that the end of the verse has. Observe the word yippelu (fall) in The peoples fall under thee (Ps. 45:6); yeminekha (thy right hand) in The Lord at thy right hand (Ps. 110:5); avdekha (thy servant) in Thou hast dealt well with Thy servant (Ps. 119:65) and many other such instances. We do not find this to be the case at the close of a verse.
AND MOSES LET HIS FATHER-IN-LAW DEPART. With respect, as in and Abraham went with them to bring them on the way (Gen. 18:16).

IN THE THIRD MONTH. We do not know the meaning of the same day (ba-yom ha-zeh) unless the interpretation of Rabbi Moses to the effect that it refers to the new moon is correct. It is like Tomorrow is the new moon (I Sam 20:18). Scripture notes this because the Torah was given a few days after Israel camped. Perhaps Moses went up to God on day one and then came down and spoke to Israel. Then on the third day of the month he went up again to report the words of the people to God. It was then told to Moses that the giving of the Torah would take place on the third day. All of this is by way of logical exegesis because we accept the tradition that the Torah was given on the sixth day of Sivan. According to the rules of the calendar, if a day was not added to the month of Iyyar, then the Torah was given on a Friday. It is possible that Scripture reads, the same day because the distance from Rephidim and Mount Sinai was greater than the distance between each journey.
AND WHEN THEY WERE DEPARTED FROM REPHIDIM. Its meaning is, they had already departed from Rephidim. I have pointed out to you many other such instances.
THEY ENCAMPED IN THE WILDERNESS. The previously mentioned wilderness of Sinai.

[AND THERE ISRAEL ENCAMPED.] Scripture reads, and there Israel encamped, after stating, they encamped in the wilderness, because the heads of the tribes and the elders camped before the mountain due to their respected positions. As I will explain, Israel stood around the mountain, in accordance with their status, on the day the Torah was given. Scripture uses the singular form va-yichan (encamped) because they were few in number. Rabbi Solomon says that before (mi-neged) the mount means on the eastern side of the mountain. However, Scripture states, a good way off (mineged) shall they pitch, round about the tent of meeting (Num. 2:2), namely, on all sides of the tent of meeting. For as the standards journeyed, so did they camp.
AND MOSES WENT UP UNTO GOD. Scripture above reads, before the mount (v. 2). Its meaning thus is: and Moses went up to the mount of God.
[AND THE LORD CALLED UNTO HIM.] Its meaning is, and the Lord had already called him. For Moses would not have ascended without permission.

[OUT OF THE MOUNTAIN.] Scripture says this becauce Moses did not ascend above the mountain. For the Lord spoke to Moses on the mountain. Do not be bothered by the fact that Scripture afterwards states, And the Lord came down upon mount Sinai (v. 20), for the Torah says this from the point of view of Israel when they beheld the cloud and fire. Scripture explicitly states, and thou didst hear His words out of the midst of the fire (Deut. 4:36).

[SAYING.] Its meaning is that the Lord called Moses to tell him: Thus shalt thou say to the house of Jacob ). The meaning is, say something relating to all of the house of Jacob, to those alive today and to their children after them.

[AND TELL THE CHILDREN OF ISRAEL.] The reference is to the elders. The elders will then tell all of the people. We thus read, And Moses came and called for the elders of the people (v. 7), and it is then written, And all the people answered together (v. 8).
[HOUSE.] I have previously explained the meaning of the word house (Ex. 1:1).

YE HAVE SEEN. The vengeance that I executed upon the Egyptians on your behalf, and that I bore you out of Egypt as if you were carried on the wings of eagles. For an eagle flies higher in the air than any other bird. All birds are afraid of him and he fears no bird. [I BORE YOU ON EAGLES’ WINGS.] Moses employed a similar metaphor later on when he said, As an eagle that stirreth up her nest (Deut. 32:11), that is, it slowly leads its young. Moses similarly referred to the clouds when he said, Spreadeth abroad her wings ( Ibid. ).

AND BROUGHT YOU UNTO MYSELF. In that God’s glory came down upon this mountain. This is the holy mountain referred to by Moses. Now Moses said, ye shall serve God upon this mountain (Ex. 3:12). The latter is the same as Thy holy habitation (Ex. 15:13).

NOW THEREFORE, IF YE WILL HEARKEN UNTO MY VOICE. To observe my commandments and keep the covenant which I will make with you. The reference, as I will explain with irrefutable proofs in the proper place, is to the covenant made by Moses with Israel after the giving of the Torah, when he built the altar.
[TREASURE.] The word segullah (treasure) means something precious, lovely, and unique.

[FOR ALL THE EARTH IS MINE.] This is connected to all peoples . The clause is to be interpreted: for all the peoples of the earth are mine. This is what Scripture means by and [I] set you apart from the peoples, that ye should be Mine (Lev. 20:26). Rabbi Merinus says that ki li kol ha-aretz (for all the earth is mine) means: even though all the earth is mine. I believe that this is the case with ki am keseh oref attah (it is a stiffnecked people) (Ex. 32:9) and refah nafshi ki chatati lakh (Heal my soul; for I have sinned against Thee) (Ps. 41:5).
AND MOSES CAME. To the camp of Israel. There is no need to mention that Moses descended.

AND SET BEFORE THEM. As in And this is the law which Moses set before the children of Israel (Deut. 4:44). However, the Gaon says that the word set is used here in the same way as the word set in set it in their mouths (Deut. 31:19). The reference is to the oral law which explains the written law.
TOGETHER. The word yachdav (together) is grammatically unique in Scripture because of the added vav . Yefet explains it to mean alone, by oneself, without anybody else there.
[REPORTED.] Scripture mentions, and Moses reported, but has no need to mention that Moses went up because Scripture is being brief.

AND THE LORD SAID. What reason is there for saying, And Moses told the words of the people unto the Lord (v. 9) after having said, And Moses reported the words of the people unto the Lord ? Note that there are many verses in the Torah that should have come earlier. Their meaning is that such and such already took place. For example, the meaning of va-yitzar (formed) in, Then the Lord God formed (Gen. 2:7) is, He had already formed; the meaning of va-yatzmach (made to grow) in And out of the ground made the Lord God to grow (Gen. 2:9) is, He had already made to grow; the meaning of va-yomer (and said) in and said: Whose daughter art thou? (Gen. 24:23) is, and he had already said. Indeed, Scripture explicitly states, And I asked her, and said (Gen. 24:47), and then, I put the ring upon her nose ( Ibid. ). Similarly, the meaning of And she said unto the servant (Gen. 24:65) is, and she had already said unto the servant, and then, she alighted from the camel (Gen. 24:64). There is no need to elaborate. Now the meaning of And Moses told here is, and Moses had already told. Scripture does not mention what Moses told. The word higid (told) always refers to something new that has not previously been mentioned. It is thus not connected to and Moses reported . From God’s answer to Moses, “ Lo, I come unto thee in a thick cloud ” (v. 9), we learn what Moses told. Furthermore, as I will explain, we find this clearly stated in Moses’ very words. Note that the Egyptians and the Indians are from the children of Ham. Each one relies on the other. The people of India do not eat meat. The Egyptians used to do the same. They changed their practice only because the kingdom of Ishmael overpowered them and they accepted the religion of the Ishmaelites. The Indian sages offer proofs in accordance with their thinking that it is impossible for God to talk to a person and for that person to live. Now the Israelites were in Egypt. There were among them people who followed this belief. They were in doubt about Moses’ prophecy. And they believed in the Lord, and in His servant Moses (Ex. 14:31) does not dispute this. For Scripture reads, And Israel saw ( Ibid. ). It does not say: and all Israel saw. Even if it read, all of Israel, it would speak of the majority as is the style of the language, as in and all the cattle of Egypt died (Ex. 9:6), which is followed by Now therefore send, hasten in thy cattle (Ex. 9:19).
[LO, I COME UNTO THEE.] This is to be understood as an answer to Moses, who told this to God.
[IN A THICK CLOUD.] When God will descend upon the mountain.
WHEN I SPEAK WITH THEE. The Decalogue. They will then believe that God in truth speaks with a person and he lives.

[AND MAY ALSO BELIEVE THEE.] That you are a prophet. All doubt will be removed from their minds. It is explicitly written, we have seen this day that God doth speak with man, and he liveth (Deut. 5:21). It is also written there, For who is there of all flesh, that hath heard the voice of the living God speaking out of the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived? (Deut. 5:23). And it is there written, Go thou near, and hear (Deut. 5:24). This is what Scripture means by and may also believe thee for ever.
AND THE LORD SAID…SANCTIFY THEM TO-DAY AND TOMORROW. Observe, God enlarged the time allotted for Israel’s sanctification by giving them the rest of this day and the morrow.

[AND SANCTIFY THEM.] By washing in water. This is indicated by and let them wash their garments. Our verse is to be interpreted after the manner of But if he wash them not, nor bathe his flesh (Lev. 17:16). Moses therefore said, starting from now, come not near a woman (v. 15) so that they would be sanctified and not be unclean. One who drew near to a women should sanctify himself, as in for she was purified from her uncleanliness (II Sam. 11:4).
AND BE READY. Its meaning might be that no person among them should sleep during the night, after the manner of the high priest on Yom Kippur, as Israel would hear God’s voice in the morning.

AND THOU SHALT SET BOUNDS. Place a border on the mount. Set bounds about the mount, and sanctify it (v. 23) is therefore similar. I dwell on this because the crazy one who inverted the words of the living God in his book said that Moses intended to say, set bounds about the people, but what came out of his mouth was “the mount” rather than “the people.”
WHOSOEVER TOUCHETH THE MOUNT. With his body.

NO HAND SHALL TOUCH HIM. The word bo (him) refers to the person who touches the mount. It means that no one shall enter after him to grab him. On the contrary, those who see him shall immediately stone him from where they are standing or shall shoot him through with arrows if he be distant.

[SHOT THROUGH.] The word yiyareh (shot through) differs from its counterparts. For the rule pertaining to roots that have a yod as their first letter is that the yod changes to a vav in the nifal imperfect, as in the word yivvada (be known) in and the plenty shall not be known (Gen. 41:31) and va-ivvaser (and I was chastised) in Thou hast chastised me, and I was chastised (Jer. 31:18). Perhaps they did this so that this root not be confused with the root of tivvare (thou mayest be feared) in That Thou mayest be feared (Ps. 130:4). For the alef and the heh are silent at the end of the word and there is no difference in pronunciation between them.
WHETHER IT BE BEAST OR MAN, IT SHALL NOT LIVE. Not so a bird as it cannot be taken, for it immediately flies away.

WHEN THE RAM’S HORN SOUNDETH LONG. Yovel (ram) is a lamb. Jubilee ( yovel ) is so called because Scripture states, Then shalt thou make proclamation with the blast of a shofar (Lev. 25:9), and the shofar is made from the horns of a lamb. It is similarly written, And it shall be, that when they make a long blast with the horn of the yovel, and when ye hear the sound of the shofar (Josh. 6:5). One must wonder at those who say that And when the voice of the horn waxed louder and louder, Moses spoke (v. 19) refers to when the ram’s horn soundeth long . For the voice of the horn was a great wonder; there was no greater wonder at that assembly around Mount Sinai. For sounds of thunder, lightning, and a thick cloud are also visible in the world. However, the voice of the horn was unheard of until the day of the Decalogue. Behold, the sound was not from the horn of a lamb.

[WHEN THE RAM’S HORN SOUNDETH LONG, THEY SHALL COME UP TO THE MOUNT.] The Gaon says that when Moses sounds the horn it will give them permission to ascend. This took place after Moses descended on the Day of Atonement and commanded that the tabernacle be constructed

THEY SHALL COME UP TO THE MOUNT. Rabbi Samuel ben Hofni says that “they” refers to Aaron, Aaron’s sons, and the seventy elders concerning whom it is written, And unto Moses He said: Come up unto the Lord, thou, and Aaron, Nadab, and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel (Ex. 24:1). However, Moses did not give permission to the rest of the people to ascend Mount Sinai. He therefore said “they” and not others. His words appear good in my sight. For the glory was continually on Sinai until the tabernacle was erected, as it is written, and the glory of the Lord filled the tabernacle (Ex. 4:34). God then spoke with Moses in the tent of meeting. Perhaps Moses then sounded the horn and now that the glory was gone, God gave him permission to ascend.
AND MOSES WENT DOWN…AND SANCTIFIED THE PEOPLE. As I have already explained.

BE READY AGAINST THE THIRD DAY. The meaning of li-sheloshet yamim is, for the third day. According to the plain meaning of the text, Moses did not add a day by himself. I will bring two faithful witnesses, both of which are found in this book. Now it is written, And he put them all together into ward three days (sheloset yamim) (Gen. 42:17). It is then written, And Joseph said unto them the third day (yom ha-shelishi) (Gen. 42:18). Scripture also states, within yet three days (sheloshet yamim) shall Pharaoh lift up thy head from off thee (Gen. 40:19). It is then written, And it came to pass the third day (ba-yom ha-shelishi) (Gen. 40:20). Similarly here, heyu nekhnim li-sheloshet yamim [means be ready for the third day].
AND A THICK CLOUD UPON THE MOUNT. Upon the mount alone. The same applies to the thunder and lightning.
[EXCEEDING LOUD.] Its meaning is, louder than the voice of any shofar (horn) that they ever heard.
AND ALL THE PEOPLE THAT WERE IN THE CAMP TREMBLED. Because of the sound of the shofar (horn).
AND MOSES BROUGHT FORTH. Its meaning is: and Moses brought forth the people out of their tents to meet God and to accept the Lord who came down on Mount Sinai as their God.

AND THEY STOOD AT THE NETHER PART OF THE MOUNT. Outside of the boundary that Moses set for them. Now they stood at Mount Sinai in a manner similar to that in which Moses made their children stand at the end of forty years when he made a covenant with them. The first-born that [ came ] near the Lord were first, after them the heads of the tribes, namely, the princes, after them the elders, after them the officers, after them all the men of Israel; after them came the little ones, after them the women, and after them the proselytes. Moses and Aaron passed over the boundary and were on the mount close to the priests. This was so even though Scripture does not explicitly say so, as Scripture was brief. We know that they did not rebel against the word of God for, behold, it is written, Go, get thee down, and thou shalt come up, thou, and Aaron with thee (v. 24). Moses similarly said, I stood between the Lord and you (Deut. 5:5).

NOW MOUNT SINAI WAS ALTOGETHER ON SMOKE. The shin of ashan (smoke) is vocalized with a long pattach because it is a verb in the perfect. Do not be surprised at the word for smoke since Scripture reads, ke-eshen ha-kivshan (as the smoke of the furnace) after saying, va-ya’al ashano (and the smoke thereof ascended). Note that ashano follows the form of shelalo (his spoil) and zehavo (his gold), for nouns come in various forms each of which has a different name. Thus Scripture reads, shegar alafekha (the increase of thy kine) (Deut. 7:13), but elsewhere it reads, ve-khol peter sheger be-hemah (every firstling that is male) (Ex. 13:12). Scripture reads, ve-et ha-bosem ve-et ha-shemen (and the spice, and the oil) (Ex. 35:28). However, we also find, ve-kinneman besem (and of cinnamon spice) (Ex. 30:23). Furthermore, Scripture reads, ariti mori im besami (I have gathered my myrrh with my spice) (Cant. 5:1). Now, if besami (my spice) was derived from bosem , the word should have been vocalized with a chataf kamatz and be pronounced bosmi like the word kodshi (my holy object), which is derived from kodesh (holy). Similarly, if besami was derived from besem (sweet) in and of cinnamon spice (Ex. 30:23), then besami should have been vocalized with a pattach like the word shamni (my oil), which is derived from shemen (oil), or with a chirik like the word tzidki (my righteousness), which is derived from tzedek (righteous). The word besami minus the yod is thus vocalized with two kematzim and pronounced basam (spice), like the word shalal (spoil) and the word zahav (gold).
AND THE WHOLE MOUNT QUAKED GREATLY. The reverse of the usual, for mountains do not move. It is only by way of parable that Scripture states, And the hills did tremble (Is. 5:25).

AND WHEN THE VOICE OF THE HORN WAXED LOUDER AND LOUDER. The normal thing is for the sound of the shofar to be stronger when first sounded. However, the reverse was the case here. Perhaps God made it sound weaker at the beginning so that Israel would not lose heart out of fright.

MOSES SPOKE. According to Saadiah Gaon, God periodically stopped the sound of the shofar, at which time Moses spoke with a loud voice. God then answered Moses with a voice, as in then he [Moses] heard the Voice speaking unto him (Num. 7:89). It is concerning this that Scripture states, that the people may hear when I speak with thee (v. 9). However, I have already told you that in my opinion, when I speak with thee refers to the Decalogue.

Moses spoke is to be explained by connecting it to the voice of the horn (shofar). Moses’ soul cleaved unto God. Moses spoke with God from the foot of the mountain and asked something of God. However, Scripture does not reveal what Moses asked. God answered Moses with a voice audible to Moses. The sound of the shofar, although very loud, did not prevent Moses from hearing the voice. Because of this, Scripture states afterwards, and the Lord called Moses with the sound of a voice and told him to ascend the mountain where the glory of God was.

AND THE LORD CAME DOWN. I will now convey a general principle that will satisfy you until, with God’s help, I will come to the Torah portion Ki Tissa, where I will explain extremely deep things to you very clearly. Know that man’s soul is extolled and glorious. It comes from the middle world. However, man’s body comes from the inferior world. The only one in this inferior world who has the ability to speak is man. Likewise the hearer, that is, the person to whom the speaker wants to convey what is in the speaker’s heart. An intelligent person cannot invent speech. He must employ the language that is known and used. All languages are built upon the arrangement of the human form, which is made up of an incorporeal soul and a body made out of four elements. Now when a person speaks to a fellow human being in a language that the latter knows, he understands the speaker’s words and their forms in their arrangements. If one wants to speak of things that are on a lower level than human beings, he has to raise their level and give them human form so that anyone who hears him will understand his words. Hence they attributed a head to the earth, as in The head of the dust of the world (Prov. 8:26), a mouth to the earth, as in And the earth opened her mouth (Num. 16:32), and a side, as in from the sides of the earth (Jer. 6:22). We similarly find, the head of the Jordan (Num. 13:29) and in the heart of the sea (Ex. 15:8). There are many such instances. Now they are all metaphoric, for the sea has no heart. Furthermore, they picture one part of the body as if it had the form of the entire body. Thus Scripture says, Death and life are in the hand of the tongue (Prov. 18:21). There are many such cases. Similarly, when a person wants to speak of things more important than he, namely, of things from the upper world, he brings them down to his level and anthropomorphizes them, speaking of them as if they had human form. All this is done so that the hearer can be understood. Scripture thus reads, the man Gabriel (Dan. 9:21). Scripture similarly speaks of his arms and his feet (Dan. 10:6) and tells us, and the voice of his words [was] like the voice of a multitude ( Ibid. ). They [the writers of Scripture] took hold of this style of speech when describing the Most High. Scripture thus states, And a helmet of salvation upon His head (Is. 59:17); For the mouth of the Lord hath spoken (Is. 1:20); The eyes of the Lord are toward the righteous, And His ears are open unto their cry; The face of the Lord is against them that do evil (Ps. 34:16,17); and and there was under His feet (Ex. 24:10). This is the way to understand And the Lord came down (Gen. 11:5) and, and God went up (Gen. 17:22), for everything is full of His glory. I will present a parable in the Torah portion Ki Tissa through which you will be able to understand what Scripture means by God ascending and descending.

[AND THE LORD CALLED MOSES TO THE TOP OF THE MOUNT.] The reason the Lord called Moses was so that Israel would see Moses’ greatly elevated state, namely, that he reached the top of the mountain where there was the glory of God, whose words the people would hear from the fire that was there.

GO DOWN, CHARGE THE PEOPLE, LEST THEY BREAK THROUGH. Each one from the place where he stands, thinking that they are rendering Me honor because of their great desire to gaze at My glory. Moses therefore said, to gaze .
[THE PEOPLE.] The term ba-am (the people) is to be read as if written twice. Our verse is to be read as if written: and shall fall from them, many people.

AND LET THE PRIESTS ALSO. The reference is to the first-born. Though the first-born are holy, as it is written, sanctify unto Me all the first-born (Ex. 13:2) nevertheless, let them add to their holiness by sanctifying themselves through their thoughts.

[THAT COME NEAR THE LORD.] Who are at the beginning of the boundary. Or its meaning is, who offered burnt offerings upon the altar that Moses built after Amalek was vanquished, and who also will offer sacrifices on the altar of the covenant that Moses built and fixed beneath the mountain where Israel stood to hear the voice of God.

AND MOSES SAID UNTO THE LORD: THE PEOPLE CANNOT COME UP TO MOUNT SINAI. Saadiah says that he contemplated this verse for many years and could not understand its meaning until he came across a book dealing with the customs of the Persian kings in which it is stated that a king’s messenger does not have permission to tell the king that he has accomplished his mission until the king commands him to do another task. Only then may he tell the king. However, I believe that because God told Moses, lest they break through unto the Lord to gaze, Moses did not know whether he had to warn the people not to gaze. He had already warned them that they were not to pass the boundary. God then told Moses, Go, get thee down and charge them as I commanded you. For Israel needed to be charged a second time.

AND THOU SHALT COME UP, THOU, AND AARON WITH THEE. A little above the boundary so as not to be too far from Israel, because after God finishes speaking the Decalogue, Israel will say to you, Speak thou with us, and we will hear (Ex. 20:16). I will now give the Gaon the answer to his question. God did not tell Moses to charge Israel not to gaze upon Him. He told Moses to charge the people not to pass over the boundary. For it was necessary to charge them at the very time of God’s revelation to listen and guard their lives.
SO MOSES WENT DOWN UNTO THE PEOPLE, AND TOLD THEM. When Moses finished telling the people, he and Aaron went up the mountain beyond the border whereupon God immediately began to speak.
